# Sound recording (phonograph, gramophone, magnetic tape) (`sound_recording`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: helped by wave_nature_light_sound, lathe_screw_cutting, mechanical_clock, electromagnetism, vacuum_tube
- Core idea: Sound makes a thin membrane vibrate. Fix a needle to the centre of a membrane at the narrow end of a horn and let it press on tinfoil or hard wax wrapped round a cylinder that is turned evenly on a screw thread, so that the needle traces a spiral: the vibrations are embossed as a wavy groove. Run the needle through the groove again at the same speed and the membrane repeats the sound. This is purely mechanical and needs no electricity. Flat discs can be pressed in thousands from one master. Later methods use a microphone and amplifier to drive the cutter, or magnetise a moving steel wire or iron-oxide coated tape with an electromagnet.
- Pitfalls:
  - Uneven turning by hand: the pitch wavers and speech becomes unintelligible; use a flywheel or governed clockwork
  - A heavy or stiff needle and membrane, which record almost nothing; they must be very light
  - Expecting high fidelity or loudness from an acoustic machine; one has to shout into the horn
  - Assuming that electricity is needed; Edison's phonograph could have been built by a good clockmaker centuries earlier
- History: europe: 1857 – Scott de Martinville's phonautograph in Paris writes sound traces on sooted paper but cannot play them back; April 1877 Charles Cros deposits a description of a reproducing machine; 1898 Poulsen's magnetic wire recorder (Copenhagen); 1935 AEG and BASF Magnetophon tape recorder (Berlin), with high-frequency bias from 1940; americas: December 1877 – Edison's tinfoil phonograph; 1886 Bell and Tainter's wax cylinder graphophone; 1887 Berliner's disc gramophone; 1925 electrical recording with microphone and amplifier (Western Electric)
- Read:
  - Oliver Read & Walter L. Welch, From Tin Foil to Stereo: Evolution of the Phonograph (1959)
  - David L. Morton, Sound Recording: The Life Story of a Technology (2004)
